Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs

How does caching (prefix/KV) help with our prompt templates?
What is the fallback behavior during capacity saturation?
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-12-22
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Zoe Patel (Redwood CSM) — Raj Patel (Ochre CTO), Elena Soto (Head Infra), Benji Morales (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Discussed p95 streaming SLOs, concurrency targets, and pilot benchmark plan. Customer needs security docs and cost model to decide between Dedicated and Private.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:06] Raj: Hi, Raj here, CTO at Ochre. We build a conversational orchestration layer for field agents, low latency is critical.
[00:11] Elena: Elena, infra. We own deployment and security.
[00:15] Benji: Benji, ML eng, we run the prompt templates and scoring.
[00:19] Maya: Great — Liam from our SE team will lead the throughput/latency portion. Liam, over to you.
[00:23] Liam: Thanks Maya. Quick agenda: current infra, target SLOs, workload shape, test plan, hosting options.
[00:30] Raj: To get straight to it, target p95 for first-byte streaming should be under 300 milliseconds for our US traffic. Completion latency can be higher but we'd like p95 end-to-end under 1s for typical 150–300 token responses.
[00:47] Liam: Okay, p95 300ms first-byte — that's a helpful target. What's your peak concurrency and average session length?
[00:56] Benji: We're looking at 1800 to 2200 concurrent active sessions during peak (US east), average response ~220 tokens, but bursts up to 800 tokens for some workflows.
[01:06] Elena: And we have to maintain data residency — some logs must remain in our VPC and we need KMS integration.
[01:12] Maya: So likely Dedicated or Private; Hosted could be an option for non-sensitive routes. Does that sound right?
[01:20] Raj: Yes. Cost is important though. We don't want to overprovision.
[01:25] Liam: Right, a few things to call out: batching and continuous streaming trade off throughput vs latency, but Redwood's runtime supports prefix/KV cache which often cuts token work for templated prompts. That helps reduce tail latency.
[01:40] Benji: When you say KV cache, do you mean the cached key/value states from previous tokens or like context prefix caching?
[01:46] Liam: Both, but in our docs KV cache sometimes shows up raw — it can be used to avoid repeating encoding work for shared prompt prefixes. We also do automatic prefix caching for common templates.
[01:54] Benji: That could be huge — we have ~70% template reuse across sessions.
[02:00] Raj: How should we size for tokens/sec? Right now a single user session averages 60 tokens/sec during streaming; with 2k sessions that's 120k tokens/sec sustained — is that realistic?
[02:12] Liam: Hmm, 120k tokens/sec sustained is a big number at the cluster level. We usually talk in terms of tokens/sec per GPU and then scale. With quantization and batching you can get a lot, but sustained 120k will need dedicated pools — probably a dozen-plus high-memory GPUs depending on model size. For 220 token responses avg, it's more common to reason about tokens/sec across the whole fleet.
[02:30] Elena: Could you ballpark tokens/sec per A100 or H100 for a 7B-ish model?
[02:36] Liam: For a 7B fp16-ish model on an H100, with efficient kernels and continuous batching you might see 6k–10k tokens/sec per card in streaming-friendly mode. For larger 13B/70B numbers drop. So to hit 120k you'd need ~12–20 cards depending on config and latency targets. But again quantization and caching can shift that.
[02:58] Raj: So Dedicated seems sensible. If we go Private on-prem, what's different?
[03:03] Liam: Private gives you full network control and meets strict residency. We ship a control plane that sits outside and a runtime in your VPC or on-prem; KMS integrations and audit logs are standard. The tradeoff is more ops overhead and longer lead times for provisioning.
[03:18] Elena: Ops overhead is fine if we can hit the p95 SLOs. We just need the runbook.
[03:23] Maya: We'll include an ops runbook and a pilot plan.
[03:26] Benji: For the pilot, how do you recommend we benchmark? We use locust for HTTP load and an internal streaming harness.
[03:34] Liam: We typically provide a 'redwood-bench' locust script that drives streaming and simulates multiplexing. Plan: baseline hosted small run to validate correctness, then Dedicated pilot window for p95 latency and tokens/sec measurement. We'll recommend steady-state runs for 20–30 minutes plus 5–10 minute bursts to catch tail behavior.
[03:50] Raj: Do you support session multiplexing so one GPU can handle many open streams? We do long-lived websockets and often many idle sessions with occasional tokens.
[03:58] Liam: Yes, we support multiplexing. The key is KV/prefix caching plus persistent KV stores to avoid recompute on idle sessions. Idle sessions don't consume as much compute until they start streaming tokens.
[04:12] Elena: If we go Dedicated, what's the SLA?
[04:16] Maya: Our Dedicated offering has SLA-backed uptime and latency objectives — we'll share the exact SLA text. For p95 latency we offer performance profiles in the model catalog with measured latencies on typical workloads.
[04:29] Raj: Can you share an example from a similar customer?
[04:32] Liam: We ran a 2-week pilot with a logistics customer that targeted p95 first-byte ~250ms at ~1500 concurrent sessions and got ~280ms consistently with similar template reuse. The main wins were prefix caching and model variant fallbacks during saturation.
[04:48] Benji: Fallbacks?
[04:50] Liam: If a high-quality 13B model would push you past capacity, we can route to a quantized 7B variant or a lower-cost region — routing policies are configurable per-route. That keeps service online albeit with a controlled quality delta.
[05:06] Elena: We need audit logs for those fallbacks and decisions for compliance.
[05:09] Zoe: Yep we can enable request-level tracing and persist decision logs; we'll include retention options.
[05:15] Raj: On security: SOC2 and SSO — we use Okta and require SCIM provisioning. Also HSM-backed KMS is a must.
[05:23] Maya: Okta SAML + SCIM provisioning and KMS/HSM integrations are supported; we'll share our security pack.
[05:28] Elena: Data deletion policies? Some of our logs have PII, need configurable retention and purging.
[05:34] Zoe: We support configurable retention windows and can mark types of logs for immediate purge on request, and we can scope what leaves your VPC in Private deployments.
[05:42] Benji: Back to benchmarking — what metric should we present internally? We need both cost per 1M tokens and p95 first-byte number under expected concurrency.
[05:51] Liam: We'll produce a benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 first-byte and completion latencies, tokens/sec sustained and burst, and estimated $/1M tokens for each hosting scenario (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). We'll also show GPU count estimates.
[06:08] Raj: How do you measure tail latency — do you include network egress? We have front-end proxies and a CDN.
[06:14] Liam: For the pilot we'll instrument from your edge (your proxy) to the model responder so you see total customer-facing latency. We'll correlate traces to separate network from model processing.
[06:24] Raj: Sounds good. One more: tokenization differences — sometimes token counts are off between our tooling and your counters.
[06:29] Benji: Yeah tokenizers differ, we use tiktoken v0.3.1 internally.
[06:33] Liam: We'll standardize on a tokenizer for bench runs; we can run your tokenizer on the same inputs to align counts.
[06:40] Elena: If the pilot shows p95 > 350ms we won't greenlight Dedicated. We'll need significant cache hits or model variant switching.
[06:48] Maya: Understood. We'll aim to get baseline numbers under 300ms.
[06:52] Raj: Ok, logistics for the pilot? What's needed from our side?
[06:56] Liam: Access to a test account (API keys), a small set of representative prompts and templates, and a reachable endpoint for the pilot region. Ideally a staging VPC for Private, or we'll provision Dedicated nodes in our hosted infra.
[07:10] Benji: We can provide those. We'll also supply users to simulate.
[07:14] Maya: Great. We'll send an email with a pilot checklist.
[07:18] (short silence)
[07:22] Raj: A question — in a saturation scenario do you queue requests or immediately fail? We need predictable backpressure semantics.
[07:30] Liam: We have configurable policies: immediate 429s, request queuing with timeouts, or model-variant fallback. For streaming, we prefer graceful fallback to maintain throughput. We'll include recommended settings for your use case.
[07:45] Elena: Is there observability at token level? We want per-token timing to analyze micro tail spikes.
[07:52] Zoe: Yes, token-level timings and per-request traces are available in Redwood Console; retention can be configured.
[07:59] Benji: How about cold-start behavior for large models? We have rare long responses that trigger cold starts.
[08:06] Liam: Cold starts for large context/large models can add 300–700ms depending on machine and sequence length; we recommend warm pools or model residency for predictable p95. Dedicated makes warm residency easier.
[08:20] Raj: Cost tradeoff then — keep more GPUs warm vs cost-per-token.
[08:24] Maya: We'll model both in the pricing deck.
[08:27] (crosstalk)
[08:30] Benji: Also wondering about model updates — how do rollouts work without impacting tail latency?
[08:34] Liam: We support canary rollouts and traffic-splitting with automatic rollback on quality regressions. You can keep a small percentage on new model and monitor prompt set evals. That minimizes blast radius.
[08:46] Raj: Nice.
[08:47] Elena: Anything else on compliance? We need penetration testing and contractual SLAs.
[08:53] Zoe: We can provide pen test evidence and incorporate SLAs in enterprise contracts; legal can follow up.
[08:59] Maya: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[09:02] Maya: Redwood to send pricing matrix, security packet, and benchmark plan. Customer to confirm pilot stakeholders and provide prompt set. Schedule pilot for Jan 4.
[09:12] Raj: Jan 4 works for us but need to lock down who will manage day-to-day.
[09:18] Benji: I'll be primary for the ML tests. Elena will own infra.
[09:22] Raj: I'll be sponsor.
[09:25] Maya: Great. Any final quick questions?
[09:28] Benji: Minor — is there prebuilt instrumentation for our prometheus stack?
[09:32] Liam: Yes, metrics exporter for Prometheus and traces for Jaeger/OTel. We'll add that to the runbook.
[09:39] Raj: Thanks everyone.
[09:41] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up by end of day Friday with docs.
[09:45] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words misheard (Redwood Dedicatede, KV cash), speaker labels sometimes simplified, filler words present.
